paragraphs: “Oh, I can’t spare the time. Please excuse me.”

“Come on, you could do your father a favor. I won’t forget it. None of you has any heart—that’s the trouble, isn’t it? What’s a day or two to you? Where are you off to now—Venice? Your Venice will keep another two days. I would have sent Alyosha, but what use is Alyosha in a thing like that? I’m sending you just because you’re a clever fellow. Do you think I don’t see that? You know nothing about timber, but you’ve got an eye. All that’s needed is to see whether the man is in earnest. I tell you, watch his beard—if his beard shakes, you know he’s in earnest.”
“So you’re making me go to that damned Tchermashnya, are you?” cried Ivan, with a malignant smile.
Fyodor Pavlovitch did not notice the malice, or did not want to notice it, but he noticed the smile.
“Then you’ll go? You’ll go? I’ll scribble the note for you right now.”
“I don’t know if I’ll go. I don’t know. I’ll decide on the way.”

“Nonsense! Make up your mind now. My dear fellow, decide! If you get it settled, jot me a line and hand it to the priest, and he’ll forward it to me right away. That’s all I’ll ask of you. Then off to Venice with you. The priest will give you horses to take you back to Volovya station.”

The old man was absolutely delighted. He wrote the note and sent for the horses. A light lunch was brought in, with brandy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch was pleased, he usually became expansive, but today he seemed to hold himself back. He did not say a word about Dmitri, for instance. The parting left him quite unmoved, and he actually seemed at a loss for something to say. Ivan noticed this particularly. “He must be sick of me,” he thought. Only when he went out with his son onto the steps did the old man start to fuss. He would have kissed him, but Ivan hurried to hold out his hand, plainly avoiding the kiss. His father saw it at once and immediately pulled himself up.
“Well, good luck to you, good luck!” he repeated from the steps. “You’ll come again sometime, won’t you? Be sure you do. I’ll always be glad to see you. Well, Christ be with you!”
Ivan got into the carriage.
“Good-by, Ivan! Don’t be too hard on me!” the father called out one last time.
Everyone in the house came out to see him off—Smerdyakov, Marfa and Grigory. Ivan gave each of them ten roubles. Once he was seated in the carriage, Smerdyakov jumped up to straighten the rug.

“You see ... I am going to Tchermashnya,” Ivan blurted out suddenly. Once more, as the day before, the words seemed to fall from his lips on their own, and he gave a strange, nervous laugh. He remembered it long afterward.
“So the saying is true, that ‘it’s always worth while speaking to a clever man,’” Smerdyakov replied firmly, with a significant look at Ivan.

The carriage rolled off. Nothing was clear in Ivan’s soul, but he gazed eagerly at the fields, the hills, the trees, and a flock of geese flying high in the bright sky. All at once he felt very happy. He tried talking to the driver and found the peasant’s answer intensely interesting. A minute later he realized that he was not taking in a word, and that he had not really understood the answer at all. He fell silent, and even so it was pleasant. The air was fresh, pure and cool, and the sky was bright. The images of Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna drifted into his mind. But he smiled gently and blew gently on the friendly ghosts, and they flew away. “There’s plenty of time for them,” he thought. They reached the station quickly, changed horses, and galloped on toward Volovya. “Why is it worth while speaking to a clever man? What did he mean by that?” The thought seemed suddenly to take his breath away. “And why did I tell him I was going to Tchermashnya?” They arrived at Volovya station. Ivan climbed out of the carriage, and the drivers crowded around him, haggling over the trip of twelve versts to Tchermashnya. He told them to harness the horses. He went into the station house, looked around, glanced at the overseer’s wife, and suddenly went straight back out to the entrance.
“I’m not going to Tchermashnya. Can I still get to the railway by seven, brothers?”
“We’ll just make it. Shall we bring the carriage out?”
“Right away. Is any one of you going to town tomorrow?”
“Sure. Mitri here is.”
“Can you do me a favor, Mitri? Go to my father’s, to Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, and tell him I haven’t gone to Tchermashnya. Can you?”
“Sure I can. I’ve known Fyodor Pavlovitch for ages.”
“And here’s something for you, since I imagine he won’t give you anything,” said Ivan, laughing gaily.
“You can count on it, he won’t.” Mitya laughed too. “Thank you, sir. I’ll be sure to do it.”

At seven o’clock Ivan boarded the train and set off for Moscow. “Away with the past. I’ve done with the old world for ever, and may I have no news, no echo, from it. To a new life, new places and no looking back!” But instead of delight, his soul was filled with a gloom, and his heart ached with an anguish, such as he had never known in his life. He spent the whole night thinking. The train flew on, and only at daybreak, as it neared Moscow, did he suddenly shake himself out of his brooding.
“I am a scoundrel,” he whispered to himself.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was well pleased to have seen his son off. For two hours afterward he felt almost happy and sat drinking brandy. Then something happened that was very annoying and unpleasant for everyone in the house, and it wrecked Fyodor Pavlovitch’s peace of mind at once. Smerdyakov went down to the cellar for something and fell from the top of the steps. Luckily, Marfa Ignatyevna was in the yard and heard him in time. She did not see the fall, but she heard his scream—the strange, peculiar scream she had known for years, the scream of an epileptic going down in a fit. No one could tell whether the fit had struck him as he was descending the steps, so that he must have fallen unconscious, or whether the fall and the shock had set off the fit in Smerdyakov, who was known to suffer from them. They found him at the bottom of the cellar steps, writhing in convulsions and foaming at the mouth. At first they feared he had broken something—an arm or a leg—and hurt himself badly, but “God had preserved him,” as Marfa Ignatyevna put it—nothing of the kind had happened. Getting him out of the cellar was hard, though. They called in the neighbors and managed it somehow. Fyodor Pavlovitch himself was present through the whole operation. He lent a hand, obviously alarmed and upset. The sick man did not come to; the convulsions stopped for a while and then started again, and everyone concluded that it would go the same way as a year before, when he had fallen from the garret by accident. They remembered that ice had been put on his head then. There was still ice in the cellar, and Marfa Ignatyevna had some brought up. In the evening Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Doctor Herzenstube, who arrived at once. He was a most estimable old man, the most careful and conscientious doctor in the province. After a thorough examination, he concluded that the fit was a very violent one and might have serious consequences. For the time being, he said, he, Herzenstube, did not fully understand it, but if the present remedies failed, he would venture to try something else by tomorrow morning. The invalid was moved to the lodge, into a room next to Grigory’s and Marfa Ignatyevna’s.

After that, Fyodor Pavlovitch had one misfortune after another to endure that day. Marfa Ignatyevna cooked the dinner, and next to Smerdyakov’s, the soup was “no better than dish-water,” and the fowl was so dried up it could not be chewed. To her master’s bitter, though deserved, reproaches, Marfa Ignatyevna answered that the fowl had been a very old one to begin with, and that she had never been trained as a cook. In the evening there was fresh trouble for Fyodor Pavlovitch: he was told that Grigory, who had been unwell for the past three days, was now completely laid up with his lumbago. Fyodor Pavlovitch finished his tea as soon as he could and shut himself up alone in the house. He was in terrible excitement and suspense. That evening he reckoned on Grushenka’s coming as nearly certain. That morning Smerdyakov had assured him “that she had promised to come without fail.” The old reprobate’s heart pounded with excitement; he paced his empty rooms, listening. He had to stay alert. Dmitri might be lying in wait for her somewhere, and when she knocked on the window (Smerdyakov had told him two days before that he had shown her where and how to knock), the door must be opened at once. She must not stand a second in the passage, for fear—God forbid!—that she might be frightened and run away. Fyodor Pavlovitch had a great deal on his mind, but never had his heart been so steeped in voluptuous hopes. This time he could say almost for certain that she would come!
